# Overview

`Optimize()` returns the coefficients it arrived at and says nothing about how
it got there. A run that stopped short of the optimum and a run that converged
look the same from the outside, as do a step size that is too small and one
that is too large.
[Callbacks](https://www.ensmallen.org/docs.html#callback-documentation) are
what `ensmallen` offers instead: objects passed as trailing arguments to
`Optimize()` and called at fixed points inside the loop, where they can print
what they are handed or keep it.

The objective used throughout is the logistic regression negative
log-likelihood built in the
[logistic regression vignette](logistic-regression.html), and the functions
called here are the ones that vignette produces. Nothing below depends on that
document having been run: the data and the reference fit are regenerated in
the next section.

```{r setup}
library(RcppEnsmallen)
```

# The fit being watched

The data are simulated from known coefficients, so there is a truth to recover
as well as an optimum to reach.

```{r data-generation}
set.seed(42)

n <- 5000
beta <- c(-1, 0.7, -0.5, 1.2)
p <- length(beta)

# Design matrix with an intercept column
X <- cbind(1, matrix(rnorm(n * (p - 1)), ncol = p - 1))

# Bernoulli responses with the logistic link
y <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = 1 / (1 + exp(-(X %*% beta))))
```

The full-batch L-BFGS fit is the reference every run below is measured
against, and `glm.fit()` confirms it independently:

```{r reference-fit}
mle <- as.vector(logistic_reg_lbfgs(X, y))
max(abs(mle - unname(glm.fit(X, y, family = binomial())$coefficients)))
```

The two agree to within the number printed above, which is small enough that a
later deviation from `mle` is a statement about the run that produced it
rather than about the implementation it came from.

# Built-in callbacks

`logistic_reg_adam()` takes a `verbose` argument, and its whole effect is to
add one callback to the `Optimize()` call:

```{Rcpp verbose-branch, eval = FALSE}
    // Callbacks are passed as trailing arguments to Optimize(). PrintLoss
    // writes to arma::get_cout_stream(), which RcppArmadillo maps to
    // Rcpp::Rcout, so the output is safe to emit from an R package.
    if (verbose) {
        optimizer.Optimize(lrf, beta, ens::PrintLoss());
    } else {
        optimizer.Optimize(lrf, beta);
    }
```

[`ens::PrintLoss`](https://www.ensmallen.org/docs.html#printloss) prints the
mean negative log-likelihood per observation once per pass over the data:

```{r verbose}
set.seed(2024)
fit5 <- logistic_reg_adam(X, y, max_epochs = 5, verbose = TRUE)
max(abs(as.vector(fit5) - mle))
```

A model that predicts one half for everything scores
$\log 2 \approx 0.693$, so that is where the optimizer sets out from. The
callback reports at the *end* of each pass, which is why the first number
printed is already below it, and the sequence falls from there.

Printing does not replace the return value. `fit5` holds the coefficients, and
the number after the five losses measures them against the maximum likelihood
estimate. Five epochs is a tenth of the fifty `logistic_reg_adam()` defaults
to, so the same step size run to the default epoch count lands somewhere else
entirely:

```{r fifty-epochs}
set.seed(2024)
fit50 <- logistic_reg_adam(X, y)
max(abs(as.vector(fit50) - mle))
```

The two deviations differ by more than an order of magnitude. What separates
an unfinished run from one that has settled on the wrong answer is the printed
sequence: five losses that are still falling when the run ends describe a
budget that ran out, not a step size that failed.

`ens::PrintLoss` writes to `arma::get_cout_stream()`, which `RcppArmadillo`
defines as `Rcpp::Rcout` rather than `std::cout`. That matters inside an R
package: output goes through R's own connection, respects `sink()`, and does
not trip the `R CMD check` warnings that writing to `std::cout` would.

Three others come up regularly:

- [`ens::StoreBestCoordinates<>()`](https://www.ensmallen.org/docs.html#storebestcoordinates)
  keeps the best parameters seen, which matters for stochastic optimizers that
  can wander away from a good point.
- [`ens::EarlyStopAtMinLoss()`](https://www.ensmallen.org/docs.html#earlystopatminloss)
  stops once the objective stops improving.
- [`ens::ProgressBar()`](https://www.ensmallen.org/docs.html#progressbar)
  reports progress on long runs.

The [full set of built-in callbacks](https://www.ensmallen.org/docs.html#built-in-callbacks)
is longer than this, and the same trailing-argument syntax accepts any number
of them at once.

# Writing your own callback

The callbacks above report on a run while it happens. A callback of your own
can keep what it sees instead of printing it, which is how the coordinates
L-BFGS passes through become available in R.

`ensmallen` does not ask a callback to inherit from a base class. It inspects
the type it is handed and calls the hooks that type defines, so a callback
implements only the hooks it needs and nothing else. The hook that records a
path is `StepTaken(optimizer, function, coordinates)`, called once after the
optimizer accepts a step, with `coordinates` holding the point that step
arrived at. Two more hooks bracket the run: `BeginOptimization()` before the
first step and `EndOptimization()` after the last, each receiving the
coordinates as they stand at that moment. A hook may return `void` or `bool`.
Returning `true` from a hook the optimizer calls inside its loop, `StepTaken()`
among them, ends the run, which is how `ens::EarlyStopAtMinLoss()` stops early.

The recorder appends what it is handed to a matrix the caller owns, one column
per point:

```{Rcpp recorder, eval = FALSE}
// Records the coordinates the optimizer passes through.
class PathRecorder
{
public:
    // The matrix to fill has one row per coefficient and no columns yet.
    explicit PathRecorder(arma::mat& path) : path(path) { }

    // Called once before the first step, with the starting coordinates.
    template<typename OptimizerType, typename FunctionType, typename MatType>
    void BeginOptimization(OptimizerType& /* optimizer */,
                           FunctionType& /* function */,
                           MatType& coordinates)
    {
        Record(coordinates);
    }

    // Called after every accepted step, with the coordinates it reached.
    template<typename OptimizerType, typename FunctionType, typename MatType>
    void StepTaken(OptimizerType& /* optimizer */,
                   FunctionType& /* function */,
                   const MatType& coordinates)
    {
        Record(coordinates);
    }

    // Called once the loop ends, with the coordinates being returned.
    template<typename OptimizerType, typename FunctionType, typename MatType>
    void EndOptimization(OptimizerType& /* optimizer */,
                         FunctionType& /* function */,
                         MatType& coordinates)
    {
        Record(coordinates);
    }

private:
    // Append one more column, unless it repeats the column already there.
    void Record(const arma::mat& coordinates)
    {
        const arma::vec point = arma::vectorise(coordinates);

        if (path.n_cols > 0 &&
            arma::all(path.col(path.n_cols - 1) == point))
        {
            return;
        }

        path.insert_cols(path.n_cols, point);
    }

    // The accumulated path, owned by the caller.
    arma::mat& path;
};
```

The hooks are templates because the optimizer type, the objective type, and the
matrix type are fixed by the call site rather than by the callback. The two
parameters each hook ignores are left unnamed, which keeps unused-parameter
warnings from firing.

`StepTaken()` takes its coordinates by `const` reference and the other two do
not, a difference the class has to reproduce exactly. `ensmallen` matches each
hook against a signature it declares in `callbacks/traits.hpp`, and one whose
qualifiers differ is not a hook it recognizes. Adding `const` to the
coordinates argument of `BeginOptimization()` compiles without a warning and
leaves that hook uncalled, so the mistake arrives as a missing column rather
than as a compiler error.

`EndOptimization()` is there because L-BFGS runs its convergence tests between
taking a step and calling `StepTaken()`. A run that stops on the last of those
tests never reports its final step, so the returned coordinates are recorded
there instead. `Record()` drops them again when `StepTaken()` has already seen
them, which is what happens when the loop exits at the top of an iteration.
Without the hook the last column comes back a step short and matches the fit
only to the convergence tolerance rather than exactly.

The exported function pairs the recorder with the objective class from the
[logistic regression vignette](logistic-regression.html#a-standalone-implementation)
and the same starting point `logistic_reg_lbfgs()` uses:

```{Rcpp logregpath, eval = FALSE}
// [[Rcpp::export]]
arma::mat logistic_reg_lbfgs_path(const arma::mat& X, const arma::vec& y,
                                  const double lambda = 0.0) {

    LogisticRegressionFunction lrf(X, y, lambda);
    ens::L_BFGS lbfgs;

    // The same zero start logistic_reg_lbfgs() uses, so the two runs agree.
    arma::mat beta(X.n_cols, 1, arma::fill::zeros);

    // One row per coefficient and no columns yet, for the recorder to fill.
    arma::mat path(X.n_cols, 0);

    lbfgs.Optimize(lrf, beta, PathRecorder(path));

    return path;
}
```

Callbacks are trailing arguments to `Optimize()`, the position
`ens::PrintLoss()` occupies in the `verbose` branch above. The recorder is
handed over as a temporary and writes into `path`, which is declared beside it
and outlives the call. A callback that keeps its result inside itself, such as
`ens::StoreBestCoordinates<>`, has to be a named object instead, and is read
after `Optimize()` returns.

The package compiles the two blocks above into `logistic_reg_lbfgs_path()`
from `src/example-logistic-regression-path.cpp`. That file carries its own copy
of the helpers and of the objective class inside an anonymous `namespace { }`,
since the L-BFGS file already defines a class of that name at namespace scope.
The standalone version of all three functions is the single file at

```{r example-path, eval = FALSE}
system.file("examples", "logistic-regression.cpp", package = "RcppEnsmallen")
```

# Recording an L-BFGS path

For a run of $k$ steps the result is a $p \times (k + 1)$ matrix whose first
column is the vector of zeros the optimizer starts from and whose remaining
columns hold the coefficients after each accepted step. Rows are coefficients
and columns are iterations, so one row is one coefficient across the whole run.

```{r path-run}
path <- logistic_reg_lbfgs_path(X, y)
dim(path)

# The last column is the fit logistic_reg_lbfgs() returned earlier.
max(abs(path[, ncol(path)] - mle))
```

With the path recorded, the surface it descends can be drawn underneath it.
Holding the first and third coefficients at their fitted values and varying the
second and fourth over a grid gives a two-dimensional slice of the objective,
which `contour()` turns into level sets. The window is centered on the optimum
and made wide enough to hold every recorded point, so the start at the origin
falls inside the frame.

```{r path-plot, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4.6, fig.alt = "Contour plot of the negative log-likelihood over the second and fourth coefficients, with the other two held at their fitted values. The level sets are closed curves nested around a single interior minimum, marked with a red cross. A blue line runs from an open circle at the origin up and to the right across the level sets, joining filled points whose spacing shrinks as they approach the cross, where the line ends."}
# Numerically stable softplus, the R counterpart of the C++ helper.
softplus <- function(e) pmax(e, 0) + log1p(exp(-abs(e)))

# Beta1 and Beta3 stay at their fitted values, so only Beta2 and Beta4 vary.
base <- X[, 1] * mle[1] + X[, 3] * mle[3]

# Grid limits: centered on the optimum, wide enough to hold the whole path.
r2 <- 1.15 * max(abs(path[2, ] - mle[2]))
r4 <- 1.15 * max(abs(path[4, ] - mle[4]))
g2 <- seq(mle[2] - r2, mle[2] + r2, length.out = 55)
g4 <- seq(mle[4] - r4, mle[4] + r4, length.out = 55)

# The negative log-likelihood at every point of the grid.
Z <- outer(g2, g4, Vectorize(function(b2, b4) {
  eta <- base + X[, 2] * b2 + X[, 4] * b4
  sum(softplus(eta) - y * eta)
}))

contour(g2, g4, Z, nlevels = 14, col = "grey65", labcex = 0.6,
        xlab = expression(beta[2]), ylab = expression(beta[4]),
        main = "L-BFGS on the negative log-likelihood")
# The optimum goes down first so the last few steps, which land on top of it,
# stay visible.
points(mle[2], mle[4], col = "#c0392b", pch = 4, cex = 1.8, lwd = 2)
lines(path[2, ], path[4, ], col = "#1b6ca8", lwd = 2)
points(path[2, ], path[4, ], col = "#1b6ca8", pch = 16, cex = 0.7)
points(path[2, 1], path[4, 1], col = "#1b6ca8", pch = 1, cex = 1.8)
legend("topright", bg = "white", box.col = "grey80", cex = 0.8,
       legend = c("Start", "L-BFGS path", "Optimum"),
       col = c("#1b6ca8", "#1b6ca8", "#c0392b"),
       pch = c(1, 16, 4), lty = c(NA, 1, NA))
```

The level sets are closed curves nested around one interior minimum. That is
the convexity the logistic regression vignette relies on when it
[starts from a vector of zeros](logistic-regression.html#a-standalone-implementation),
in the form a two-dimensional plot can carry it: restricting a convex function
to two of its arguments leaves a convex function, so a slice showing two
separate basins would contradict the claim, while this one is consistent with
it.

Two qualifications come with the picture. The path runs through all $p$
coefficients and the plot draws two of them, so points sitting close together
here can be further apart in the coordinates not shown. The surface underneath
also holds the first and third coefficients at their fitted values, which the
early iterates had not reached, so the contour a point sits on is not the
objective value the optimizer saw when it was there.

The first step covers most of the distance and the later ones crowd together
around the optimum. L-BFGS stops once the objective stops improving rather than
after a fixed number of iterations, which is why `dim(path)` reports around a
dozen columns instead of hundreds.
